t: Longest Chunked Palindrome Decomposition — Greedy Two-Pointer Matching
o: We must cut `text` into k consecutive pieces so that piece i equals piece k-i+1 (the whole sequence reads the same forwards and backwards at chunk level). We want the maximum k, which means we want as many small chunks as possible. The key observation: greedily match the shortest possible prefix with an equal suffix. In "antaprezatepzapreanta", matching (a)...(a) first leaves a smaller subproblem in the middle; any optimal decomposition can be transformed into one that makes this earliest shortest match without losing chunks. Constraints (n ≤ 1000) allow O(n²) approaches, but a rolling-hash or direct comparison greedy gives near-linear behavior.
k: Greedy works: always peel off the shortest prefix that equals the current suffix — each such pair contributes 2 to k.
If no proper prefix of the remaining string matches its suffix, the whole remainder is one middle chunk (+1) and we stop.
The problem is self-similar: after removing matched prefix/suffix pairs, the same procedure applies to the inner substring.

a.n: Approach 1: Greedy Two Pointers with Direct Comparison
a.i: Keep two pointers l and r on the current unmatched window. For each candidate length len = 1..(window/2), check whether text[l:l+len] == text[r-len+1:r+1]. The first (shortest) match is safe to take greedily: taking it can never reduce the total count because any valid decomposition's outermost pair must cover these characters anyway, and splitting earlier only adds opportunities. If no length up to half the window matches, the entire window becomes one final middle chunk.
s: While l < r, try lengths len = 1, 2, ... while l+len-1 < r-len+1.
On the first match text[l..l+len-1] == text[r-len+1..r], add 2 to the answer, move l += len, r -= len, restart len search.
If no length matches before pointers cross, add 1 for the middle chunk and stop.
a.t: O(n²) worst case — each greedy step may scan up to half the window with substring comparisons; with n ≤ 1000 this is fast in practice.
a.sp: O(1) extra space beyond slicing (O(n) transiently in Python/JS slices).

a.i: Same greedy structure, but instead of comparing substrings character by character, maintain forward hash of the prefix and backward hash of the suffix incrementally. When hashes match (optionally verify once to avoid collisions), we accept the chunk pair. This reduces each candidate comparison to O(1), giving expected linear time overall.
s: Use base B and large modulus M; keep hashF of text[l..l+len-1] and hashB of text[r-len+1..r].
For each new len, update hashF = (hashF * B + text[l+len-1]) % M and hashB = (hashB + text[r-len+1] * pow(B, len-1)) % M.
When hashF == hashB, accept: add 2, reset both hashes and power term, advance l and shrink r.
If pointers cross without a match, add 1 for the middle chunk.
a.t: Expected O(n) — each character participates in O(1) hash updates per accepted chunk boundary; hashing comparisons are O(1).
a.sp: O(n) for precomputed powers of the base (or O(1) if computed on the fly).

w: In an interview, lead with Approach 1: it is simple, obviously correct, and comfortably fits n ≤ 1000. Mention the greedy exchange argument (peeling the earliest shortest equal prefix/suffix pair never hurts) since that is the crux. Pitfalls: forgetting the odd middle chunk when no match exists (answer must be at least 1); off-by-one in the condition `l + len - 1 < r - len + 1` ensuring the two halves don't overlap; assuming the longest match is needed — shortest is what maximizes k. Follow-ups: prove greedy optimality formally, handle n up to 10⁶ (use rolling hash / Z-function / suffix structures), or handle strings where verification against hash collisions matters.
